name: Wolff's law facial loading

lead: Wolff's law is a nineteenth-century principle that bone adapts its structure to the loads placed on it. In looksmaxxing it is the reasoning behind mewing, chewing, thumb pulling and bonesmashing: if bone responds to load, then loading the face should build a stronger jaw and more prominent cheekbones.

The general principle, now usually called bone functional adaptation, is supported by research on limbs and the spine. Bone cells sense strain and signal bone-forming and bone-resorbing cells, and Frost's mechanostat model describes strain thresholds for adding or losing bone. Whether the small, specific forces of tongue posture, chewing or pulling change the adult facial skeleton has not been tested.

paras: People apply it by choosing practices that load the face, such as tongue posture, hard chewing or pulling on the palate, and by tracking changes in photos. It is a rationale rather than a routine of its own.
The principle itself carries no risk. Practices justified by it, such as forceful pulling or striking the face, have their own risks and are covered on their own pages.

angle.text: Wolff's law, the real principle that bone remodels to the loads it carries, is the logic behind mewing, chewing and pulling practices aimed at a stronger jaw and cheekbones. Applying it to adult facial bone with these methods has not been tested.

lead: Wolff's law is the principle that bone adapts to the loads placed on it: it becomes denser and stronger where loading increases and weaker where loading falls [1][2]. It is named for the German anatomist and surgeon Julius Wolff (1836-1902), whose 1892 book Das Gesetz der Transformation der Knochen set the idea out [2]. In looksmaxxing, Wolff's law is the scientific reference point behind facial-loading practices: mewing and tongue posture, hard chewing, thumb pulling and bonesmashing are all justified on the reasoning that if facial bone responds to force the way a tennis player's racquet arm does, the forces applied to the face can improve jaw, cheek and chin structure [3].

The principle itself is well established in bone biology and is now usually called bone functional adaptation; reviewers note that Wolff's original mathematical formulation has been discredited while the broader concept of adaptation to loading is supported by a large body of experimental and observational data [4]. Frost's mechanostat model describes how strain thresholds switch bone modeling and remodeling on and off [5][6][7]. For the face, research on the jaw is largely animal-based: rats and mice fed soft diets develop smaller or differently shaped mandibles than animals fed hard diets [8], and a review of masticatory muscle research links stronger chewing function to specific mandibular shapes [9].

What has not been published is a study showing that tongue posture, chewing exercises, pulling or striking changes the facial skeleton of an adult. A six-month randomised trial of gum-chewing training in 58 adults raised bite force but did not change masseter thickness or mandibular shape [10]. How facial-loading practices relate to the principle, and where the evidence stops, is set out below.

paras: When loading on a bone increases, the bone remodels over time to resist it; when loading decreases, it loses density. Reduced loading, for example in astronauts under microgravity, leads to bone loss [2]. Only cyclic loading is described as inducing bone formation [2].

Wolff's concept built on earlier work, and Harold Frost later refined it as the mechanostat and the Utah paradigm, which propose strain thresholds. In one formulation, strains below about 50 microstrain accompany the largest disuse effects, while strains above about 1500 microstrain tend to turn on bone modeling that adds and reshapes bone [6][7]. A reviewer for clinicians argues that remodeling alone can remove or conserve bone but not add it, with modeling responsible for adding bone [6].

Mechanical effects on bone depend on the magnitude, rate and duration of loading. Duncan and Turner's 1995 findings, as summarised on Wikipedia, were that only cyclic loading induces bone formation, which is why steady static pressure and varied dynamic loading are discussed differently in the literature [2]. Everyday examples used to illustrate the principle include the dominant arm of tennis players, which has stronger bone than the other arm, weightlifters' increased bone density and astronauts' loss of bone in microgravity [2].

Julius Wolff (1836 to 1902), a German anatomist and surgeon, set out the idea in his 1892 book Das Gesetz der Transformation der Knochen, which received an English translation in 1986.[2] Wikipedia notes that the internal trabecular structure of bone changes first under altered load and the outer cortical bone afterwards, and that computational models suggest mechanical feedback can reorient trabeculae along load directions.[2]

Reduced loading can weaken bone; clinicians use the term stress shielding for the loss that can follow a hip replacement, when an implant carries load that bone formerly bore.[2] Wikipedia also notes that nothing shows a broken bone heals stronger than before, which corrects a popular misreading of the law.[2] Harold Frost's Utah paradigm, or mechanostat, is presented there as a refinement of Wolff's law, and the article cites a 2008 paper on craniofacial bone grafting titled Wolff's Law Revisited and a 1994 Frost overview in The Angle Orthodontist, which place the principle within skull and jaw research.[2]

For appearance, this is the idea behind facial-loading practices: if the jaw and face respond to the forces on them as other bones do, then changing habitual forces (chewing, tongue posture, growth guidance in children) could in principle change facial form over time. Proponents argue this; researchers describe bone adaptation to load as well established in general and note that studies of whether home practices in adults change facial bones have not been published.[4][7]

Wikipedia traces Wolff's work to earlier drawings of the internal structure of bone by the engineer Karl Culmann and the anatomist Hermann von Meyer, who observed that the trabeculae in the femoral head lie along lines resembling engineering stress trajectories [2]. Wolff's 1892 statement was mathematical and deterministic. In the twentieth century and after, authors such as Harold Frost reframed it: his 1990 papers redefined it as the modeling and remodeling problems [11], his 1994 overview for orthodontists set out how modeling and remodeling differ [6], and his 2003 update tied it to the cell mechanisms known by then [7]. A 2006 paper on anthropological use of the term concluded that the mathematical law is discredited but that bone functional adaptation is supported [4].

Remodeling works through mechanotransduction, in which cells convert mechanical signals into biochemical ones. Osteocytes, the most abundant bone cells, are particularly sensitive to fluid flow caused by loading and signal other cells [2]. Mechanically sensitive proteins such as PIEZO1 regulate bone homeostasis through osteoblast and osteoclast signalling in mouse research [12].

In the mechanostat model, bone strain is compared with set points. Very low strain, as in disuse, brings bone loss next to marrow; normal and high usage conserve bone; and strains above roughly 1500 microstrain tend to switch on modeling that adds bone, according to Frost's formulation as presented in clinician reviews [6][7]. Reviews also note that adaptation is most active in growing bone and responds mainly to high-magnitude, high-rate strains in unusual distributions rather than to the small, steady loads of daily life [13].

At the cell level, osteocytes embedded in bone sense fluid flow induced by loading and signal osteoblasts and osteoclasts [2]. The mechanically sensitive channel PIEZO1 has been shown in mouse studies to regulate bone homeostasis through osteoblast-osteoclast crosstalk, an example of the molecular detail now added to Wolff's descriptive law [12].

The jaw is a load-bearing bone: orthodontic reviews list the mandible and maxilla among bones adapted to chewing forces [7]. Researchers have studied how the loading from chewing shapes the face, mostly in animals. A 2015 study by Hichijo and colleagues raised ten three-week-old rats on either hard pellets or soft powdered food for 11 weeks and found that the soft-diet mandibles had a shorter ramus, larger gonial and ramus angles and a smaller overall size, with lower bone volume at the condyle and masseter attachment; the authors described the changes as region-specific and the sample was five animals per group [8].

Kiliaridis's 1995 review of animal and clinical work reported that the elevator muscles of the jaw influence the width and height of the face, and that stronger masticatory function is associated with a forward-rotating mandibular growth pattern and well-developed angular, coronoid and condylar processes [9]. Work on diet consistency has not been uniform: some studies report narrower maxillae with soft diets and others no significant effect [8][9]. This research concerns growing animals and children's jaw development, not adults performing home exercises.

Mewing, named for the British orthodontist John Mew and popularised by his son Mike Mew, holds that resting the tongue against the roof of the mouth shapes the jaws and face; Wikipedia describes interest rising from January 2019 and spreading through social media and looksmaxxing communities [3]. Its supporters often frame it through bone adaptation to habitual force. The American Association of Orthodontists states there is no evidence that mewing improves the jaw, and Wikipedia describes the practice as unproven [3]. Mike Mew was erased from the UK dental register by the General Dental Council in November 2024 after a conduct panel found some of his approaches not sufficiently supported by scientific evidence and likely to cause harm; he has criticised the regulator and appealed [14][15].

Hard gum, tough foods and resistance jaw trainers are adopted on the reasoning that more masseter work means more bone loading. The only randomised trial found in adults, from Yonsei University (Jung and colleagues), assigned 58 healthy adults to chew gum three times a day for six months or to no training. Maximum bite force and occlusal contact area rose at three months, while masseter thickness and mandibular shape showed no statistically significant change [10].

Thumb pulling, bonesmashing and similar methods apply brief or impact forces directly to facial bone. Researchers describe bone modeling as responding to dynamic, high-rate strain, and the mechanostat framework also recognises that excess strain can cause microdamage [6]; no study has measured the strain these practices produce in facial bones or their effect on appearance.
No studies found testing Wolff's law or bone loading as applied to do-it-yourself facial reshaping through tongue posture, pulling or striking.

Related research: the 2024 randomised gum-chewing trial in 58 adults found increased bite force and occlusal contact area with no significant change in masseter thickness or mandibular shape over the follow-up [10]. Animal work on diet consistency shows region-specific differences in mandibular bone and shape in growing rats [8], and reviews of masticatory muscle function link it to face dimensions and mandibular growth patterns [9]. General bone-adaptation research includes anthropological and clinician reviews supporting bone functional adaptation [4][7] and a study correlating wrist loads with distal radius tilt in 30 wrists.

Proponents of mewing and related practices argue that facial bones are shaped by forces applied over time. One forum guide lists as premises that facial structure is moulded by forces, that facial sutures never fuse, and that forward growth of the maxilla is the goal. Critics in the same discussions and orthodontic bodies say these claims have not been demonstrated; the American Association of Orthodontists states there is no evidence mewing reshapes the jaw [3].

lore.intro: 'Wolff's law' is invoked in looksmaxxing forums as scientific backing for mewing, chewing, pulling and bonesmashing, often alongside the argument that facial sutures never fuse. Orthotropics and mewing discussion on social media carries the same bone-adaptation reasoning [3][14].

claims.claim: Facial bones remodel under mechanical load, so loading the face can reshape it
Facial sutures never fuse, so adults can still grow the face
Greater force means more bone change

Tongue posture reshapes the maxilla and jaw in adults
Wolff's law means bone always grows stronger where stressed
Reduced chewing load, such as soft modern diets, underdevelops the jaw
